Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Akua had always taken pride in her work as a fisherman, braving the unpredictable waters off the coast of Louisiana. But it was on one fateful day three years ago that her life took a devastating turn. Her 10-year-old son, Kofi, had been involved in a horrific car accident on his way home from school, leaving him with severe injuries and a long road to recovery. Akua's world crumbled around her as she watched her vibrant child struggle to regain his strength. As the anniversary of the accident approached each year, Akua found herself becoming increasingly withdrawn. She would lie awake at night, replaying the events leading up to the crash, wondering if there was anything she could have done differently to prevent it. "If only I had driven him to school that day," she would think, her mind consumed by an endless cycle of what-ifs. These anniversaries became a painful reminder of her perceived failures as a mother. Conversations about accidents or crashes also triggered Akua's distress. She would become agitated and try to change the subject, unable to bear the thought of reliving that terrible day. Even seeing cars damaged in accidents on the side of the road would send her spiraling into a state of anxiety, her heart racing as she envisioned Kofi's fragile body being torn apart. Akua tried to cope with these feelings by spending money impulsively, hoping to distract herself from the crushing guilt and self-blame. She would buy unnecessary gifts for Kofi or splurge on lavish dinners, but the fleeting sense of comfort only left her feeling emptier and more anxious in the long run. Her sleep patterns suffered as well; she found herself staying up until the early hours of the morning, her mind racing with thoughts of what could have been done differently. Akua's irritability grew, causing tension in her marriage. She would lash out at her husband over minor issues, feeling like she was drowning under the weight of her own inadequacies. Her strong negative emotions made it difficult for her to connect with others, including Kofi, who needed her support more than ever. As a fisherman, Akua's work took her out on the water, but even the familiar rhythms of the sea couldn't calm her mind. She felt like she was constantly on edge, waiting for the next disaster to strike. Her body would react physically whenever something reminded her of the accident – her heart racing, her palms growing sweaty. Akua's greatest fear was that she had failed to protect Kofi, and this sense of failure haunted her every waking moment. She couldn't shake the feeling that if only she had done things differently, the accident might have been prevented. This self-blame had become a constant companion, eroding her confidence as a mother and a person. As the years went by, Akua's relationships began to fray. Her husband felt helpless in the face of her growing anger and withdrawal, while Kofi sensed his mother's lingering sadness but didn't know how to reach out to her. It was only when Akua realized that she was starting to push away the people she loved most that she knew she needed help. With a deep sense of trepidation, she reached out for therapy, hoping to find a way to break free from the cycle of guilt and self-blame that had consumed her life.
